title: Python's int never overflows -- until you explicitly ask for a fixed-width one
assumption: An integer type has some maximum size, and adding to it eventually overflows or errors.

input.description: Serializing a Python int into a fixed-width binary format (a network protocol, a C-compatible struct, a file format) where the field is a 32-bit signed integer, after the value has grown past what that field can hold.

what_goes_wrong: Code that works fine for years because Python's `int` just keeps growing starts failing (or, worse, silently wraps to a negative number) the moment that same value has to be packed into a fixed-width field for serialization, networking, or C interop -- and which of those two happens depends entirely on which API you used to do the packing.
why: Python's built-in `int` is arbitrary-precision: it has no fixed bit width and never overflows on its own. Fixed-width behavior only appears when you explicitly convert to one -- `struct.pack` with a format like `"i"` (the platform's C `int`, signed 32-bit on all mainstream platforms) validates the range and raises `struct.error` if the value doesn't fit, while `ctypes.c_int32` instead performs a real two's-complement modulo-2^32 wraparound, silently producing a negative value with no error at all. The two standard-library tools for 'give this a fixed width' disagree on whether out-of-range is an error or a wraparound.

repros.code:
import struct
import ctypes

try:
    struct.pack("i", 2**31)
except struct.error as e:
    print("struct.pack raises:", e)

print("ctypes.c_int32 wraps silently:", ctypes.c_int32(2**31).value)
print("plain python int, unaffected:", 2**31)
repros.expected_output:
struct.pack raises: 'i' format requires -2147483648 <= number <= 2147483647
ctypes.c_int32 wraps silently: -2147483648
plain python int, unaffected: 2147483648

fix: When serializing a Python int into a fixed-width field, validate the range yourself first (or use `struct.pack` and handle the `struct.error`) rather than reaching for `ctypes`, whose wraparound is silent and easy to miss in a code review.
